newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: American named as investigator for Kabila's Congo.
newsitem.headline: American named as investigator for Kabila's Congo.

text.p: An American human rights expert, Reed Brody, was named on Friday as the third member of a U.N. team probing alleged massacres of Rwandan refugees in President Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said in a statement that the mission would meet in Geneva on Aug. 13-15 and then leave for Kinshasa. He previously named two African experts for the controversial mission, formed after Kabila refused to let a previous U.N. rights team into the country.
Brody was director of the human rights division in the U.N. peacekeeping mission in El Salvador and executive director of the International Human Rights Law Group.

Previously Annan named Atsu-Koffi Amega of Togo, a supreme court judge, and Andrew Chigovera, the deputy attorney general of Zimbabwe, to head the mission. It has been delayed for months because of Kabila's objections to a critical report from Roberto Garreton, a Chilean human rights lawyer.

The refugee crisis followed the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of Tutsis and moderate Hutus by militant Hutus. More than a million Rwandan Hutus crossed into what was then Zaire, fearing reprisals by Tutsis who have taken over the government.

Most returned home, but U.N. relief officials say up to 200,000 are missing. Kabila's forces, aided by Rwanda, seized power in Kinshasa in May, deposing veteran president Mobutu Sese Seko. He denied his Tutsi supporters were responsible for the alleged killings.
